MHHS2401 · Musculoskeletal System · Lecture 22

Muscles of the Trunk thoracic wall, abdominal wall, and how the spine moves

Every lecture slide is shown in full and explained the way a tutor would. The lecture wraps the trunk in two layers: the thoracic wall, where intercostal muscles close the gaps between ribs and move them for breathing, and the abdominal wall, where three flat muscles cross at angles like plywood and their aponeuroses wrap the rectus abdominis. It then brings back the back muscles from L21 to explain why each region of the spine moves the way it does.

How to use this guide

Each slide is shown in full (click to enlarge). The note underneath is not a re-caption. It adds the action, the nerve, and the clinical or landmark point. For every muscle ask three things: what does it attach to, what does it do, and which nerve supplies it? For the spine, ask what limits movement in that region.

§1LO1 · Muscles of the thoracic wall

The thoracic wall and its muscles

A ribbed cylinder closed by muscle, moved for breathing.

The trunk is the body minus the head, neck and limbs. Its upper part, the thorax, is a cage of ribs whose gaps are filled by three layers of intercostal muscle, with the nerves and vessels running in a protected groove.

Orientation · bone above, muscle below

Slide 5 is the map for the whole lecture. Above the costal margin, the trunk wall is mostly bone (ribs) with muscle in the gaps. Between the costal margin and the pelvis (iliac crest, inguinal ligament) there is almost no bone, so the abdominal wall is entirely muscle and aponeurosis: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, with quadratus lumborum, psoas major and iliacus behind. That difference explains why the abdomen can expand (eating, pregnancy, breathing) and the chest can't.

Why · a cylinder with a lid and a floor

The thorax is an irregularly shaped cylinder. It has a narrow superior thoracic aperture (rib 1, manubrium, T1), through which trachea, oesophagus and great vessels pass to the neck, and a wide inferior thoracic aperture closed by the musculotendinous diaphragm. Its musculoskeletal wall protects heart and lungs while still moving for breathing. Inside are three compartments: the left and right pleural cavities (lungs) and the central mediastinum (heart, great vessels, oesophagus, trachea).

Exam hook · muscles that sit on the chest but aren't "thoracic wall"

Several upper-limb muscles attach to the ribs: pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius, serratus anterior (shoulder lectures, wk1). With the arm fixed (e.g. hands on knees), they can lift the ribs, which is why breathless patients brace their arms (the "tripod position"). Serratus posterior (superior and inferior) and levatores costarum, deep back muscles, are accessory respiratory muscles. The true thoracic wall muscles are the intercostals, subcostales and transversus thoracis.

Why · three layers, and a protected groove

Each intercostal space is closed by three muscle layers. External intercostals run down and forward (the "hands in pockets" direction) and mainly elevate ribs (inspiration). Internal intercostals run at right angles to them and mainly depress ribs (forced expiration). Innermost intercostals run in the same direction as the internal layer. The intercostal nerve, artery and vein run in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above, between the internal and innermost layers, in the order V-A-N (vein, artery, nerve) from top to bottom. All intercostal muscles are supplied by intercostal nerves (anterior rami T1–T11).

Clinical · where to put the needle

Because the neurovascular bundle hugs the inferior border of each rib, chest drains and pleural taps go in just above the upper border of the rib below, avoiding the vessels and nerve. The safe site for a chest drain is the "triangle of safety" in the 4th–5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line. An intercostal nerve block is placed at the lower border of the rib for rib-fracture pain.

Why · the innermost layer's extensions

Both lie in the same plane as the innermost intercostals, completing the deepest layer. Subcostales lie on the inner posterior wall, are more numerous lower down, and can span more than one intercostal space; they elevate ribs. Transversus thoracis lies on the deep surface of the anterior wall (from sternum to costal cartilages), deep to the internal thoracic vessels, which it holds against the wall; it depresses ribs. Both are supplied by intercostal nerves.

R Recall — thoracic wall
  • Thoracic cavity compartments — two pleural cavities and the mediastinum
  • Inferior thoracic aperture is closed by — the diaphragm
  • Upper-limb muscles attached to ribs — pectoralis major/minor, subclavius, serratus anterior
  • Accessory respiratory back muscles — serratus posterior, levatores costarum
  • Intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between — internal and innermost intercostals, in the costal groove
  • Order in the costal groove (top to bottom) — vein, artery, nerve
  • Subcostales — posterior wall, elevate ribs
  • Transversus thoracis — anterior wall, deep to internal thoracic vessels, depresses ribs
§2LO2 · Abdominal wall — structure

Layers of the abdominal wall and its posterior muscles

From skin to peritoneum, and the muscles that line the back of the abdomen.

The abdominal wall is built in layers, and those layers are the order you cut through in surgery. Its muscles fall into posterior, lateral (anterolateral) and anterior groups.

Exam hook · the layers, outside to in

Skin → superficial fascia (fatty Camper's and membranous Scarpa's layers) → muscles and their deep fascia → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum. Its skeletal frame is the 5 lumbar vertebrae and IV discs behind, the upper pelvic bones below, and the lower thoracic cage above. A midline incision passes through only skin, fascia, the linea alba, transversalis fascia, fat and peritoneum, with no muscle fibres, which is why it bleeds little.

Why · one continuous wall of different muscles

Posterior (beside the vertebral column): quadratus lumborum, psoas major, iliacus. Lateral (anterolateral): three layers, external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis. Anterior: the segmented rectus abdominis. They are joined into one continuous wall by fascia posteriorly (thoracolumbar fascia) and by the flat tendinous sheets (aponeuroses) of the lateral muscles anteriorly. A fascial layer (transversalis fascia) separates the muscles from the peritoneum.

Exam hook · posterior wall: attachments, action, nerve

Psoas major: from the T12–L5 vertebral bodies, discs and transverse processes, to the lesser trochanter. It flexes the hip (with iliacus as iliopsoas) and flexes the trunk (bilaterally) or bends it laterally. Nerve: anterior rami L1–L3. Psoas minor (absent in ~40%) is a weak trunk flexor. Iliacus: from the iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter with psoas, hip flexor, supplied by the femoral nerve. Quadratus lumborum: from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament to rib 12 and the lumbar transverse processes. It fixes rib 12 in inspiration and laterally flexes the trunk. Nerve: anterior rami T12–L4.

Clinical · the psoas sign

Psoas lies directly behind the appendix (right) and the kidneys. When an inflamed appendix or a psoas abscess irritates it, extending the hip stretches psoas and causes pain (the psoas sign), and patients lie with the hip flexed. A psoas abscess (classically spinal TB) can track down within the psoas sheath and appear as a lump in the groin below the inguinal ligament.

R Recall — abdominal wall structure
  • Deepest layer of the abdominal wall — parietal peritoneum
  • Abdominal wall skeletal elements — 5 lumbar vertebrae, upper pelvic bones, lower thoracic cage
  • Posterior wall muscles — quadratus lumborum, psoas major, iliacus
  • Three lateral layers — external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
  • Anterior segmented muscle — rectus abdominis
  • Psoas major nerve — anterior rami L1–L3
  • Quadratus lumborum attaches to — rib 12 and iliac crest
§3LO2 · Anterolateral muscles, aponeuroses and rectus sheath

The anterolateral abdominal muscles and the rectus sheath

Three flat muscles crossing like plywood, wrapped around a central strap.

Five muscles make up the anterolateral wall. Three flat sheets become aponeuroses near the midline, and those aponeuroses form the rectus sheath around the two vertical muscles.

Why · fibres at three angles make a strong wall

The three flat muscles start posterolaterally and run forward, becoming aponeuroses toward the midline. External oblique fibres run down and medially ("hands in pockets"). Internal oblique fibres run up and medially, at right angles to the external oblique. Transversus abdominis fibres run horizontally. Like plywood, the crossed layers resist forces from every direction, which makes a thin but strong, flexible wall. Near the midline lie two vertical muscles enclosed in a tendinous sheath: rectus abdominis and the small pyramidalis (which tenses the linea alba and is absent in some people).

Exam hook · actions and nerves

All four compress and support the abdominal viscera and assist (forced) expiration, by raising intra-abdominal pressure and pushing the diaphragm up. External and internal obliques flex and rotate the trunk. Transversus abdominis compresses (the "corset" muscle, key to core stability). Rectus abdominis flexes the trunk. Nerves: the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami T7–T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12) supply all of them. Internal oblique and transversus also receive L1 (iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal).

Why · the six-pack

Rectus abdominis runs from the pubic crest and symphysis to the xiphoid and costal cartilages 5–7. It is crossed by usually three tendinous intersections fused to the front of its sheath, which divide it into the visible segments. The segmented design reflects its origin from several body segments and lets parts contract separately. The lower fibres of the flat muscles also form the walls of the inguinal canal, and the lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament.

Exam hook · the arcuate line switch

Above the arcuate line (about a third of the way from umbilicus to pubis), the internal oblique aponeurosis splits: the anterior layer joins the external oblique aponeurosis in front of rectus, and the posterior layer joins the transversus aponeurosis behind it. Below the arcuate line, all three aponeuroses pass in front, so the back of rectus lies directly on transversalis fascia. The aponeuroses meet in the midline at the linea alba, where fibres cross from one side to the other.

Why · the two sides are one muscle sheet

At the linea alba, aponeurotic fibres cross the midline: superficial fibres from one side run deep on the other (intramuscular exchange within the external obliques), and the right external oblique continues into the left internal oblique (intermuscular exchange). The left and right obliques therefore act as one continuous diagonal sling. Rotating the trunk to the right uses the left external oblique together with the right internal oblique, the "synchronous" action in the slide 28 table.

Clinical · where leaked urine goes

The membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa's fascia) continues into the perineum as Colles' fascia, around the penis as the superficial penile fascia, and into the scrotum as the dartos. It is firmly attached to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament and to the ischiopubic rami. So if the spongy urethra ruptures (e.g. a straddle injury), extravasated urine spreads into the scrotum, penis and up the anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs. The attachments act as barriers.

R Recall — anterolateral wall
  • Number of anterolateral muscles — 5 (3 flat, 2 vertical)
  • Two vertical midline muscles — rectus abdominis and pyramidalis
  • Muscles that flex and rotate the trunk — external and internal obliques
  • Muscle that mainly compresses and supports viscera — transversus abdominis
  • Nerves of the anterolateral muscles — T7–T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal (+ L1)
  • Below the arcuate line — all aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus
  • Midline meeting of the aponeuroses — linea alba
  • Scarpa's fascia continues as — Colles' fascia in the perineum
§4LO2 · Blood and nerve supply of the abdominal wall

Blood supply, nerves and dermatomes of the abdominal wall

A vessel and nerve plane between internal oblique and transversus.

The abdominal wall's vessels and nerves travel in one plane, between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, the same plane as the intercostal bundle above.

Why · two arteries meet in the sheath

The neurovascular bundle runs between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, continuous with the intercostal plane (§1). Within the rectus sheath, the superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic) runs down and the inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac) runs up, and they anastomose. That link between subclavian and iliac territories can bypass a blocked aorta (coarctation). The lateral wall is also fed by the 10th–11th posterior intercostal and subcostal arteries, the musculophrenic, and the deep and superficial circumflex iliac and superficial epigastric arteries.

Clinical · rectus sheath haematoma

Coughing, injections or anticoagulants can tear an epigastric artery inside the sheath. Above the arcuate line the haematoma is contained by the posterior sheath. Below it, it can spread more widely, mimicking an acute abdomen. Surgeons placing laparoscopic ports lateral to rectus aim to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels.

Exam hook · the dermatome landmarks

Nerves: anterior rami T7–T11 (thoracoabdominal nerves, the continuations of the intercostal nerves), T12 subcostal, and from L1 the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves. Dermatome landmarks: T4 at the nipple (in males), T10 at the umbilicus, T12 suprapubic, L1 at the inguinal region. Remember "T10 = belly but-TEN".

Clinical · referred pain and shingles

Because the same spinal segments supply viscera, early appendicitis pain is felt around the umbilicus (T10) before it moves to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes involved. Shingles (herpes zoster) follows a single dermatome as a band of painful rash around one side of the trunk. A low transverse (Pfannenstiel) incision can injure the iliohypogastric or ilioinguinal nerves, causing numbness or groin pain.

R Recall — blood and nerve supply
  • Neurovascular plane — between internal oblique and transversus abdominis
  • Arteries anastomosing in the rectus sheath — superior and inferior epigastric
  • Anterior wall nerves — anterior rami T7–T11, T12 subcostal, iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal
  • T10 dermatome — umbilicus
  • T4 dermatome — nipple (males)
  • L1 dermatome — inguinal region
§5LO3 · Movements of the back

Movements of the vertebral column — region by region

Disc thickness and facet orientation decide what each region can do.

This section brings back L19–L21. Each region's mobility follows from its discs and facet orientation, and each movement is produced by a predictable set of back and trunk muscles.

Why · mobility comes from the discs, direction from the facets

Movement varies by region and between individuals. It comes mainly from the compressibility and elasticity of the IV discs. Its range is limited by: disc thickness (thicker relative to the body means more motion); the shape and orientation of the articular processes (which steer the movement); facet joint capsule tension; and the resistance of back muscles and ligaments (ligamenta flava, posterior longitudinal ligament). It is assisted by the anterolateral abdominal wall and gravity.

Exam hook · neck movers

The cervical spine is free because its discs are thick relative to the small vertebral bodies, its facets are almost horizontal and large, its capsules are loose, and the slender neck has no surrounding bulk. Flexion is greatest in the neck. Flexion (bilateral): longus colli, scalenes, sternocleidomastoid. Extension (bilateral): splenius capitis and cervicis, semispinalis capitis and cervicis. Lateral bending (unilateral): iliocostalis cervicis, longissimus capitis and cervicis, splenius. Rotation (unilateral): rotatores, semispinalis, multifidus, splenius cervicis. Bilateral contraction gives flexion or extension; one side alone gives bending or rotation.

Why · the ribs lock the thoracic spine

In the thoracic region rotation is the main free movement. The discs are thin relative to the vertebral bodies, the articular processes are vertical (the facets lie roughly on an arc centred on the vertebral body, which allows twisting but suppresses flexion and extension), and the ribs and sternum brace the region. The rib cage provides stability and protects the thoracic organs at the cost of mobility.

Clinical · why the lower back takes the strain

Lumbar discs are thick, so flexion and extension are free. Extension is greatest in the lumbar region. But the facets face each other (sagittally) and interlock, so rotation is blocked. Twisting while bent forward and lifting combines a lot of flexion with an attempt to rotate a segment built to resist it. This is the classic mechanism for lumbar disc herniation, usually posterolateral at L4/5 or L5/S1, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrowest (L20).

Exam hook · trunk movers (back + abdomen together)

Flexion (bilateral): rectus abdominis, psoas major, and gravity. Standing up, flexion is mostly the back extensors lowering you eccentrically (L21). Extension (bilateral): erector spinae, multifidus, semispinalis thoracis. Lateral bending (unilateral): iliocostalis, longissimus, multifidus, external and internal obliques, quadratus lumborum. Rotation (unilateral): rotatores, multifidus, and the external oblique acting together with the opposite internal oblique (the sling from slide 18), plus semispinalis thoracis.

Synthesis · no movement uses one muscle

Real movements recruit whole chains. Lateral flexion uses splenius, sternocleidomastoid, iliocostalis and longissimus, the obliques, quadratus lumborum, and even rhomboids, serratus anterior and the glutei to stabilise. Rotation pairs the transversospinalis group with the external and internal obliques. Starred muscles in the figure take part in the overall movement without acting on the IV joints themselves. This is the point of LO3: back (L21) and trunk (L22) muscles work as one system around the spine (L19–L20).

R Recall — movements of the back
  • Spinal mobility comes mainly from — IV disc compressibility and elasticity
  • Movement is assisted by — the anterolateral abdominal wall and gravity
  • Region with greatest flexion — cervical
  • Main free movement of the thoracic spine — rotation
  • Region with greatest extension — lumbar
  • Why lumbar rotation is limited — interlocking articular processes
  • Trunk flexors — rectus abdominis, psoas major, gravity
  • Trunk extensors — erector spinae, multifidus
  • Trunk rotation by the obliques — external oblique with the opposite internal oblique
